extracted.intended_audience: early-career researchers and grant applicants (graduate students, postdocs, early-career faculty)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice on emotional and behavioral steps for researchers to recover after a grant rejection, framed as six stages of 'scientific grief' and culminating in practical action (revising and resubmitting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond with class
rubrics_metrics.description: “First of all, I take the news with a class not seen since the likes of Grace Kelly or Jackie O.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice to maintain professionalism and composure when receiving rejection. The author immediately caveats this with humor, implying realistic expectations, but emphasizes that how you handle the news matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage one: The initial let down
rubrics_metrics.description: The anxious wait for the decision and the shock when the rejection email arrives; the full weight of the rejection hasn’t quite hit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and accept the immediate emotional impact: frequent checking, disbelief, and early denial are normal first reactions before you can begin processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage two: Justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Telling anybody who will listen (or your computer screen) about why you should have been funded — emphasising your breakthrough technology, model, or noble intentions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a relatively short phase where you rationalize and defend your proposal; be aware it tends to include martyrdom and fuels the move into anger. Expect it, but don’t let it derail productive next steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage three: Anger
rubrics_metrics.description: Becoming angry at the perceived poor judgment of reviewers and questioning how they were selected for the review committee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anger is a normal stage; it's part of processing the setback. Acknowledge it but don’t act destructively on it—it typically gives way to other emotions that allow recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage four: Pride
rubrics_metrics.description: Realizing your ideas were clever and cutting-edge and concluding that reviewers simply didn’t understand them; possibly convincing yourself you didn’t really want the funding if it meant being associated with short-sighted reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is labelled 'dangerous' — inflated pride can prevent honest self-appraisal. Treat it as a phase to move through rather than a permanent stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage five: The temper tantrum
rubrics_metrics.description: A period of intense ranting and emotional outburst (humorously described as going 'full Tasmanian devil' with possible spitting and throwing of objects) that signals movement forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although extreme emotions may surface, this phase indicates you are processing; loosen the grip on anger, allow the moment to pass, and prepare to return to rational work and revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage six: Acceptance (and rewrite)
rubrics_metrics.description: The calm after the storm when you begin to see some of the reviewers’ points, agree with a few, and are ready to retrieve your laptop, make coffee, and rewrite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptance is the productive stage: use the perspective gained to revise your proposal, incorporate reviewer feedback where appropriate, and prepare a stronger resubmission.
